title: Unified title
summary: This paper investigates backdoor attacks on LLMs by studying diffusion models from a transition-dynamics perspective, proposing Normal Diffusion Dynamics Learning (NDDL) as a novel framework for backdoor defense. The paper demonstrates that optimization-induced differences can lead to hidden backdoors, and introduces the Universal Optimization Backdoor (UOB) to address this issue.

sources.title: SoK: Systematizing LLM Prompt Security: Taxonomies, Datasets, and Unified Evaluation of Attacks and Defenses
sources.description:
arXiv:2510.15476v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Prompt-security claims for large language models (LLMs) are often compared as properties of individual attacks or defenses, although measured harmfulness depends on the target model, access setting, attack and defense configuration, prompt sample, and judger. We systematize 272 studies through three linked, multi-label taxonomies of jailbreak attacks, defenses, and model vulnerabilities. To make these dependencies explicit, we introduce an access-compatible evaluation protocol over configured $\langle M,A,D,S,J\rangle$ tuples and instantiate it in PromptSecurity, an open-source platform that records method settings, outputs, judgments, and query costs. We release two complementary datasets: JailbreakDB, with 445,752 jailbreak system-user prompt pairs and 1,094,122 benign prompts, and PromptSecurity-Eval, with 166,200 harmful-query and 9,200 benign-utility output records. We evaluate 11 target models, 20 attacks, nine defenses, and three automated judgers under a matched, single-turn protocol using 100 harmful queries and separate benign-utility tasks. Lower attack success can reflect failure to execute transformed requests rather than stronger safety; attack-category advantages can reverse when one method is excluded, and attack success varies with assistant choice. Defenses can reduce harmful outputs while degrading benign-task utility or causing backfire. Rejudging identical outputs also shows that measured attack success is sensitive to the behavior supplied to the judger, highlighting the need to report judger configurations alongside ASR. These findings motivate configuration-aware reporting rather than context-free method rankings.
  Leaderboard: https://datasec-lab.github.io/PromptSecurityLeaderboard/. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/youbin2014/JailbreakDB. GitHub: https://github.com/datasec-lab/PromptSecurity.

sources.title: A Few Steps Further: Why Defenses Against Malicious Finetuning Erode Under Continued Training
sources.description:
arXiv:2605.14605v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Model providers increasingly release the weights of large language models. Although these models are safety-aligned before release, their safeguards can often be removed by fine-tuning on harmful data. A growing class of defenses aims to make alignment robust to such malicious fine-tuning, but these defenses are typically evaluated against attacks with a fixed training budget, even though an attacker who holds the weights can simply train for longer. We ask whether current defenses withstand this simplest escalation. Surveying fifteen recent defenses, we find that they share a common weakness: each is built around a limited model of the attacker, such as a bounded perturbation, a short simulated attack, or a trained link between harmful and benign behavior, and nothing enforces that protection once the weights are released. We then test six representative defenses on four open-weight models by continuing the same harmful-only fine-tuning attack for three epochs and measuring harmfulness and capability along the way. In all 72 defended runs, the model is more harmful at the end of training than at release, and on Llama-3.1 at the highest learning rate the defended models end almost as harmful as the undefended one. The defenses are not equally weak: one defense kept harmfulness low on one model, and some attacks recovered harmfulness only at the cost of general capability. Current defenses can delay or disrupt malicious fine-tuning, but in most cases their measured resistance does not persist under continued training, and they should not yet be treated as durable protection.
